artifact.recommendation: Adopt regional token buckets with bounded global quotas and a local burst allowance.
reasoning: Regional enforcement avoids adding the 180 ms p99 cross-region control-plane path to request admission and preserves availability during regional dependency failures.
Bounded regional allocations limit how much of shared capacity any tenant can consume globally, addressing the concentration where 2% of tenants generate 61% of peak traffic.
A local burst allowance can absorb observed short bursts of up to 4× the five-minute average while reducing customer-visible false throttling.
Existing regional entitlement replicas can supply quota inputs without a synchronous global lookup.
This design can be implemented with one regionalized stateful limiter dependency, fitting the stated operational budget better than a globally centralized critical-path service.
considerations: Allocate each tenant a global quota split across regions, plus explicitly capped regional burst credits.
Use adaptive quota rebalancing outside the request path for tenants whose traffic shifts between regions.
Fail open only within strict emergency ceilings so partitions preserve service without allowing unbounded tenant consumption.
Define token-bucket capacity and refill rates from entitlement, observed burst duration, and shared-capacity headroom.
Instrument per-tenant throttles, regional allocation exhaustion, burst-credit use, and estimated global overshoot.
assumptions: Active-active routing may send a tenant's traffic to multiple regions concurrently.
Regional quota allocations can be refreshed asynchronously and cached through control-plane outages.
The one-new-stateful-dependency budget permits a limiter datastore or service deployed regionally as one logical platform dependency.
Small bounded quota overshoot during partitions is preferable to stopping all requests.
risks: Static regional splits can falsely throttle a tenant in one region while unused allocation remains elsewhere.
Partition-time local allowances can produce bounded global quota overshoot.
Adaptive rebalancing may oscillate or lag during abrupt traffic shifts.
A shared regional limiter dependency can become a regional bottleneck unless it is highly available and capacity-tested.
Generous burst allowances may let a large tenant briefly pressure shared capacity.
evidence_needed: Per-tenant traffic distribution and failover behavior across the three regions.
Available shared-capacity headroom during simultaneous 4× bursts from top tenants.
Acceptable partition-time quota overshoot and emergency fail-open policy.
Limiter datastore throughput, latency, availability, and recovery benchmarks under peak load.
Simulation results comparing false-throttle rates for candidate regional allocation and burst parameters.

citations.claim: The top 2% of tenants generate 61% of peak-hour request volume, supporting enforceable per-tenant bounds.
Frequent bursts reach 4× average for under 20 seconds, supporting local burst capacity.
Cross-region control-plane round trips have 180 ms p99 latency, arguing against centralized request-path admission.
An 11-minute regional dependency outage occurred while application instances remained healthy, supporting region-local partition tolerance.
The platform team can support at most one new stateful dependency, constraining operational complexity.
Regionally replicated tenant entitlement data can provide quota inputs without a new global lookup.

artifact.recommendation: Adopt regional token buckets with bounded global quotas and a local burst allowance.
reasoning: This architecture best balances tenant isolation, partition availability, latency, and operational capacity.

Allocate each tenant a bounded quota per region, with controlled redistribution through an asynchronous control plane; this limits the capacity any tenant can consume globally without putting cross-region coordination on the request path.
Size local burst capacity to absorb the observed short spikes—frequently 4× the five-minute average for under 20 seconds—reducing costly false throttling.

Regional enforcement continues during a cross-region partition, unlike a centralized limiter, while bounded allocations avoid the effectively unbounded aggregate overshoot possible with independent per-instance buckets.
Existing regional entitlement replicas can supply quota inputs without a synchronous global lookup or another globally critical dependency.
considerations: Use a token bucket per tenant and region, with refill rates derived from entitlements and regional allocations.
Keep global quota allocation asynchronous and off the request path; cap regional leases so partitions cause only bounded overshoot.
Support temporary regional borrowing or periodic allocation rebalancing for active-active traffic shifts, but impose hard ceilings and lease expiry.
Define explicit degraded-mode behavior during control-plane partitions, preserving already leased capacity and local burst tokens.
Add safeguards for the highest-volume tenants because a small cohort dominates peak load.
The design should require no more than one new stateful dependency, ideally deployed regionally with a narrowly scoped control plane.
assumptions: Tenant traffic can be attributed reliably before rate-limit enforcement.
Global quotas may tolerate small, explicitly bounded overshoot during allocation lag or partitions.
Entitlement changes do not require instantaneous global enforcement.
Active-active routing can shift tenant traffic between regions, so static equal allocation alone would create false throttling.
Regional limiter state can remain available independently when cross-region connectivity fails.
risks: Poor regional allocation may throttle a tenant in one region despite unused quota elsewhere.
Excessive local burst allowances or stale leases can permit meaningful global overshoot during partitions.
A hot tenant may create high-cardinality state or contention in the regional limiter.
Control-plane or entitlement lag may delay quota changes.
The regional stateful implementation could exceed the five-person team's operational capacity if redistribution and reconciliation are over-engineered.
evidence_needed: Per-tenant traffic distribution and failover behavior across the three regions.
Shared-capacity limits and the maximum acceptable global quota overshoot during partitions.
Tenant-specific burst distributions, not only the aggregate 4× observation.
Expected entitlement update frequency and required enforcement delay.
Benchmarks for the proposed regional state store under peak cardinality, hot-key load, and regional failure.
Simulation results comparing false-throttle and overshoot rates during routing shifts and an 11-minute partition.

citations.claim: The top 2 percent of tenants generate 61 percent of peak-hour request volume, making strong per-tenant isolation important.
Bursts frequently reach 4 times a tenant's five-minute average for less than 20 seconds, supporting a local burst allowance.
Cross-region control-plane p99 latency is 180 ms, arguing against synchronous global coordination on each request.
A regional dependency outage lasted 11 minutes while application instances remained healthy, supporting partition-tolerant local enforcement.
The platform team can support at most one new stateful dependency, constraining architectural complexity.
Regionally replicated tenant entitlements can provide quota inputs without a new global lookup.

strengths: The recommendation directly addresses the stated tradeoffs among tenant isolation, partition availability, request latency, false throttling, and team capacity.
The report uses all six supplied evidence items and maps them to relevant architectural implications.
Keeping cross-region coordination asynchronous and off the request path is well supported by the 180 ms p99 cross-region latency.
Regional quota bounds combined with local burst allowances are a credible response to both concentrated tenant demand and short 4× traffic bursts.
The report explicitly recognizes allocation imbalance, stale leases, hot-key contention, entitlement lag, bounded overshoot, and operational over-engineering as risks.
The evidence-needed section appropriately calls for simulations and benchmarks before committing to detailed parameters.
weaknesses: The proposal remains conceptual: it does not specify quota-allocation formulas, lease duration, refill intervals, burst-bucket sizing, redistribution cadence, or overshoot bounds.
It does not clearly define whether the regional limiter is centralized per region, distributed among API instances, or embedded in an existing stateful service.

The statement that the design should require no more than one new stateful dependency does not demonstrate that the proposed data plane, control plane, reconciliation, and lease management can actually meet that constraint.
The recommendation does not quantitatively compare expected false-throttling, overshoot, latency, availability, or operational cost across the three options.
The local burst recommendation extrapolates from an aggregate observation without showing that a single bucket policy works across tenants with materially different traffic profiles.
unsupported: The claim that a single globally centralized limiter would not continue during a cross-region partition is not established; its behavior depends on placement, replication, routing, and failure policy.

The claim that independent per-instance buckets permit effectively unbounded aggregate overshoot is directionally plausible but requires assumptions about instance count, autoscaling limits, and bucket initialization.

The assertion that temporary regional borrowing can remain bounded is incomplete without a concrete lease protocol, expiry semantics, clock assumptions, and behavior during delayed or duplicated control-plane messages.
The conclusion that the architecture best fits operational capacity is not substantiated by an implementation or ownership model.
missing: A numerical definition of the global quota invariant and the maximum acceptable overshoot during normal operation, allocation lag, and an 11-minute partition.
A precise burst-sizing policy, including whether burst capacity derives from entitlement rate, observed traffic, service capacity, or tenant tier.
Explicit fail-open, fail-closed, and stale-state behavior for limiter-store failures, entitlement failures, control-plane failures, and complete regional isolation.
A mechanism for reserving shared service capacity and preventing the sum of tenant burst allowances from overwhelming downstream systems.
Details on atomic token consumption, consistency, replication, recovery, lease fencing, clock skew, and duplicate-request handling.
A plan for tenant identity resolution and protection against missing, spoofed, or excessively high-cardinality tenant keys.
Treatment of autoscaling, regional evacuation, retries, hedged requests, and routing oscillation, all of which can amplify consumption or false throttling.
Operational requirements such as observability, per-tenant diagnostics, emergency overrides, rollout strategy, configuration validation, and rollback.
A concrete comparison with simpler variants that might reuse an existing regional stateful dependency and better satisfy the five-person-team constraint.
incorrect_assumptions: The assumption that active-active routing can shift each tenant's traffic between regions is plausible but not provided by the evidence; active-active routing alone does not establish tenant-level mobility or its magnitude.
The assumption that regional limiter state remains available independently is a design requirement, not an established property; it depends on the selected store and deployment topology.
The assumption that entitlement changes need not be enforced instantly is unverified and could be invalid for abuse response, contract downgrades, account suspension, or security incidents.
The assumption that bounded quota overshoot is acceptable has not been confirmed or quantified against shared-capacity safety requirements.
critical_risks: Aggregate local burst allowances could exhaust shared capacity even when every tenant remains within its individual policy, defeating a central decision requirement.
Regional allocation imbalance during traffic shifts could cause expensive customer-visible false throttling unless borrowing is both fast and safely bounded.
A partition lasting as long as the observed 11-minute outage could produce substantial quota overshoot if leases or burst tokens are sized too generously.
The proposed distributed quota and lease machinery may exceed the team's operational budget despite nominally using only one new stateful dependency.
Incorrect lease recovery or fencing could double-allocate quota after failover and violate global bounds.
recommended_changes: Define measurable acceptance criteria: maximum false-throttle rate, maximum global overshoot, limiter latency budget, regional availability target, and protected shared-capacity headroom.
Specify the architecture concretely, including regional store topology, token-consumption atomicity, global allocator ownership, lease lifecycle, fencing, expiry, and reconciliation.
Derive regional allocations and burst sizes from per-tenant and per-region traces, then test routing shifts and an 11-minute partition through simulation.
Add a separate aggregate regional capacity guard so valid per-tenant bursts cannot collectively overload shared infrastructure.
Document a failure-mode matrix covering regional store loss, control-plane partition, entitlement staleness, clock skew, failover, autoscaling, and recovery.
Prototype and benchmark the design under peak tenant cardinality and hot-key load before confirming that it fits the one-dependency operational constraint.
Compare all three options quantitatively, including explicitly defined implementations and failure policies, rather than rejecting broad architectural categories categorically.

strengths: The recommendation directly addresses all three core constraints: tenant isolation, partition availability, and limited operational capacity.
The reasoning is well tied to the supplied evidence, especially burst behavior, cross-region latency, workload concentration, and regional entitlement replication.
The report explicitly recognizes the principal tradeoff: regional autonomy improves availability but permits bounded overshoot and can cause false throttling when allocations are uneven.
The proposed local burst allowance appropriately targets the observed 4× bursts lasting under 20 seconds.
Keeping adaptive rebalancing outside the request path is a sound way to avoid cross-region latency becoming request-admission latency.
The evidence-needed section correctly calls for traffic-distribution data, capacity headroom analysis, datastore benchmarks, and simulations before parameter selection.
The fail-open recommendation includes emergency ceilings rather than allowing unlimited traffic during partitions.
weaknesses: The architecture remains conceptual: it does not specify quota-allocation mathematics, token-bucket parameters, synchronization frequency, or overshoot bounds.
It treats a regionally deployed limiter as one logical stateful dependency without explaining whether each region requires an independent cluster and how that affects operational burden.
The report does not clearly distinguish entitlement limits, fairness limits, and protection of aggregate shared capacity; these may require different controls.
The statement that regional enforcement preserves availability during regional dependency failures is too broad because the proposed regional limiter can itself become such a dependency.
No quantitative comparison is provided against the other two options for latency, availability, false-throttle rate, overshoot, or operating cost.
Adaptive rebalancing is proposed without defining stability controls, stale-allocation behavior, or safeguards against allocation duplication.
unsupported: The claim that bounded regional allocations will limit a tenant's global consumption is only valid if allocations cannot be duplicated and their sum remains bounded under retries, stale state, failover, and concurrent rebalancing.
The claim that the design fits the operational budget is not established without a deployment and ownership model for three regional limiter installations plus their control plane.
Evidence e4 establishes a prior regional dependency outage, but does not by itself show that a regional limiter architecture will remain available during comparable failures.
The preference for small partition-time overshoot over rejecting requests is plausible but is not explicitly established by the problem statement or quantified business requirements.
The recommendation assumes that one common burst policy can reduce false throttling without demonstrating that simultaneous bursts from high-volume tenants fit available capacity.
missing: A precise definition of the global quota semantics, including whether limits are hard contractual ceilings or capacity-protection targets.
Quantified maximum overshoot during an 11-minute partition, including contributions from all three regions and emergency allowances.
A method for sizing refill rates, bucket capacities, regional shares, and burst credits using e2 and actual shared-capacity headroom.
An aggregate regional or service-wide overload guard to protect shared capacity when many individually compliant tenants burst simultaneously.
Behavior for limiter datastore failure, timeout, degraded performance, restart, state loss, and recovery reconciliation.
A routing and failover analysis covering retries, tenant traffic moving between regions, and double consumption during failover.
A concrete comparison table or experiment contrasting all three candidate architectures against the decision criteria.
Operational details such as high availability, replication model, observability objectives, latency budget, capacity planning, and rollback strategy.
Fairness and abuse controls for tenants using multiple credentials, endpoints with different costs, or deliberately distributed regional traffic.
incorrect_assumptions: It is not established that the one-new-stateful-dependency constraint counts a multi-region limiter service and its supporting control plane as only one dependency.
It is not established that quota allocations can be refreshed asynchronously and remain safe throughout control-plane outages; that is a design requirement requiring validation.
The assumption that bounded overshoot is acceptable may be wrong if tenant quotas are contractual, billing-sensitive, or tied to strict downstream capacity limits.
The report implicitly assumes request cost is uniform; simple request-count token buckets may not protect capacity when endpoints have materially different resource costs.
critical_risks: Incorrect or stale regional allocations could duplicate quota and turn nominally bounded overshoot into sustained global overuse.
The regional limiter could become a new critical-path bottleneck or single point of regional failure, recreating the availability problem the design aims to avoid.
Static splits or slow rebalancing could create costly false throttling during regional traffic shifts even when global tenant quota remains available.
Simultaneous burst allowances for dominant tenants could exhaust shared capacity despite each tenant remaining within its local bucket.
Fail-open ceilings that are not quantitatively derived could either permit damaging overload or reject excessive legitimate traffic during an extended partition.
Rebalancing races, retries, and active-active failover could cause double spending unless quota-transfer semantics are carefully designed.
recommended_changes: Define explicit decision criteria and quantitatively score all three options for admission latency, partition availability, tenant isolation, false throttling, overshoot, and operational complexity.
Specify the quota invariant: the sum of steady regional allocations plus maximum emergency exposure must remain within a stated global bound.
Provide formulas and example values for refill rate, bucket depth, regional allocation, and burst credits, then test them against the observed 4×/20-second bursts.
Add hierarchical controls: per-tenant regional buckets combined with regional aggregate capacity guards and, where needed, endpoint-weighted request costs.
Document allocation-transfer semantics that prevent duplication, including epochs or leases, idempotency, stale-state handling, and conservative behavior during rebalancing.
Define failure modes separately for control-plane partition, regional limiter outage, datastore latency, state loss, and routing failover, with bounded fail-open behavior for each.
Validate the design through trace-driven simulation using tenant-by-region traffic and failure scenarios; report false-throttle rates, maximum overshoot, and capacity saturation.
Benchmark a candidate regional limiter implementation at peak and burst load, including failover and recovery, before confirming that it fits the five-person team's operational budget.
State whether quotas are contractual hard limits or capacity-management limits, because that determines whether any partition-time overshoot is permissible.

attacks: The recommendation is not yet an architecture; it omits the regional store topology, global allocator, lease protocol, fencing, atomic token consumption, and recovery semantics needed to prove quotas remain bounded.
Calling three regional deployments plus allocation, reconciliation, and failover machinery “one logical dependency” obscures operational burden and may violate the five-person-team constraint.

Per-tenant regional buckets do not by themselves protect shared capacity: simultaneous allowed bursts—especially from the dominant 2%—can overload downstream systems while every tenant remains policy-compliant.
Static allocations risk costly false throttling when traffic shifts regions; rapid borrowing reduces that problem but introduces duplication, oscillation, stale leases, and partition-time overshoot.

The 4×-for-20-seconds observation does not justify a universal burst allowance. It lacks tenant-level distributions, concurrency data, endpoint costs, and evidence that aggregate capacity can absorb correlated bursts.
“Bounded global quotas” is unsupported until the design proves that allocations cannot be duplicated during retries, failover, stale updates, clock skew, or allocator recovery.
Regional enforcement does not automatically preserve availability: the proposed regional limiter becomes a new request-path dependency and could reproduce the cited regional dependency outage.

The claimed advantage over a global limiter relies on an underspecified straw implementation. A globally managed limiter could use regional replicas, leased quotas, or local degraded modes; the alternatives were not compared as concrete designs.

Emergency fail-open ceilings create an unresolved contradiction: ceilings low enough to protect capacity may cause false throttling, while ceilings high enough to preserve customer traffic may defeat tenant isolation.

Simple request-count buckets assume requests have comparable resource cost. Expensive endpoints or distributed credentials could let a tenant exhaust shared compute while staying under its request quota.

The design conflates contractual entitlement enforcement, tenant fairness, abuse control, and aggregate overload protection; these require different invariants and possibly hierarchical or weighted controls.
The very high recommendation confidence is unjustified before trace simulation, failure testing, capacity measurements, and an operational prototype resolve the acknowledged unknowns.
falsifiers: Trace-driven simulation shows regional allocation plus safe borrowing cannot meet the required false-throttle target during normal routing shifts or regional evacuation.
The worst-case sum of steady allocations, burst credits, stale leases, and emergency allowances exceeds protected shared-capacity headroom during an 11-minute partition.
A prototype cannot meet request-path latency and availability objectives under peak cardinality, top-tenant hot keys, store failover, and recovery.
Failure injection demonstrates duplicate quota allocation or double spending during allocator failover, delayed messages, retries, lease expiry, or clock skew.
Operational assessment shows the three regional data planes and global allocation/reconciliation plane require more than one supportable stateful dependency or exceed team on-call capacity.
Tenant-by-region traces show traffic is sufficiently stable and region-affine that a simpler regional policy performs equivalently, making adaptive global allocation unjustified.
Capacity data shows correlated 4× bursts from major tenants cannot be admitted safely even with an aggregate guard, invalidating the proposed burst allowance.
Business requirements establish quotas as strict contractual, billing, security, or abuse ceilings with zero permissible overshoot during partitions.
Endpoint-cost analysis shows request counts correlate poorly with resource consumption, so unweighted token buckets fail the shared-capacity protection objective.
A concretely designed centralized or existing-infrastructure-based alternative achieves equal partition availability and lower false-throttling or operational cost.
evidence_gaps: Quantified acceptance thresholds for false throttling, global overshoot, admission latency, availability, and reserved shared-capacity headroom.
Per-tenant, per-region traffic traces covering normal operation, routing changes, regional evacuation, retries, and correlated bursts.
Tenant-level burst distributions and concurrency, rather than only the aggregate 4×/20-second observation.
A numerical quota invariant and worst-case overshoot calculation for normal lag, control-plane partition, regional limiter loss, and the observed 11-minute outage.
Concrete formulas and example values for regional shares, refill rates, bucket depths, lease duration, redistribution cadence, and emergency ceilings.
Shared-capacity measurements showing whether simultaneous compliant bursts can be supported; no aggregate regional overload guard is specified.
A precise deployment and ownership model demonstrating that the regional stores, allocator, reconciliation, and failover mechanisms fit the one-dependency budget.
Benchmarks for peak throughput, tenant cardinality, hot-key contention, latency, replication failure, restart, state loss, and recovery.
Failure semantics for store timeout or outage, stale entitlements, complete regional isolation, allocator failure, clock skew, delayed messages, and duplicate requests.
Quota-transfer correctness evidence, including epochs or fencing, idempotency, lease expiry, and prevention of double allocation.
Clarification whether quotas are hard contractual limits, billing controls, abuse limits, or soft capacity-management targets.
Endpoint resource-cost data and a policy for weighted requests, multiple credentials, missing or spoofed tenant identity, and high-cardinality keys.
A quantitative comparison of concrete implementations of all three options, including their degraded modes and reuse of existing dependencies.
Rollout, rollback, observability, per-tenant diagnostics, configuration validation, emergency override, and capacity-planning requirements.

accepted_criticisms: The recommendation is directionally sound but underspecified: it lacks a concrete regional-store topology, quota invariant, allocator/lease/fencing protocol, atomic consumption semantics, and recovery behavior.
Treating a multi-region limiter and its allocation/reconciliation control plane as one logical dependency does not establish that it fits the five-person team's operational budget.
Per-tenant buckets alone cannot protect shared capacity when many compliant tenants burst simultaneously; an aggregate regional capacity guard is required.

Adaptive allocation creates material risks of duplicate allocation, stale leases, oscillation, and partition-time overshoot, while static allocation can cause costly false throttling during routing shifts.
The 4×-for-20-seconds aggregate observation is insufficient to select a universal burst allowance without tenant-level traces, concurrency, endpoint-cost, correlation, and capacity-headroom data.
The claim of bounded global quotas requires a numerical invariant and correctness mechanisms covering retries, failover, stale state, allocator recovery, and clock behavior.
A regional limiter remains a request-path dependency and therefore needs an explicitly defined degraded mode; regional placement alone does not preserve availability during its own outage.
The alternatives were not compared as concrete implementations with equivalent degraded modes, so the advantage over a centralized design was overstated.
Emergency ceilings cannot be selected responsibly without quantified capacity headroom and acceptable false-throttling and overshoot thresholds.
Uniform request-count buckets may not protect shared compute when endpoint costs differ materially.
Entitlement enforcement, tenant fairness, abuse prevention, and aggregate overload protection require distinct controls or a hierarchical policy.
The original confidence of 0.94 was too high before trace simulation, failure injection, capacity benchmarks, and operational validation.
rejected_criticisms: The missing implementation proof does not by itself make another listed option preferable. A synchronous global limiter conflicts with the 180 ms cross-region latency and partition-availability evidence, while uncoordinated per-instance buckets cannot provide meaningful global tenant bounds.
The evidence does support a local burst mechanism in principle because short 4× bursts are frequent; it does not support a universal or specifically sized burst allowance.
The one-stateful-dependency constraint does not conclusively disqualify a regionalized limiter service, although compliance remains unproven until its deployment and ownership model are assessed.
artifact.updated_recommendation: Retain regional token buckets with bounded global quotas as the leading option, but make adoption conditional on validation. The concrete design should combine endpoint-weighted per-tenant regional buckets with regional aggregate capacity guards; use fenced, idempotent, leased allocations whose steady shares and maximum emergency exposure satisfy an explicit global bound; and define conservative degraded behavior for control-plane partitions and regional limiter failures. Before commitment, compare concrete implementations of all three options, run tenant-by-region trace simulations and failure injection, benchmark the request path, quantify false throttling and worst-case overshoot over an 11-minute outage, and verify that the complete multi-region deployment fits the team's operational budget. If quotas are strict contractual ceilings with zero permissible overshoot, reject partition-time fail-open and reconsider the architecture.
reasons: The supplied evidence still favors local request-path enforcement: cross-region control-plane latency is 180 ms p99, and a partition must not stop all requests.
Per-instance uncoordinated buckets remain unable to enforce a defensible tenant-wide bound across instances and regions.
Regional entitlement replicas reduce the need for synchronous global lookups and support a regional design.
The criticism exposes missing mechanisms and measurements that are essential to establish boundedness, capacity protection, failure availability, and operational feasibility.
The recommendation therefore remains the best-supported direction among the stated options, but it is not yet a proven production architecture and warrants substantially lower confidence.

accepted_criticisms: The report is too conceptual to establish bounded global quotas; it lacks a concrete regional-store topology, allocator, lease lifecycle, fencing, atomic token consumption, and recovery semantics.

The one-new-stateful-dependency constraint is not demonstrated. Regional data planes plus allocation, reconciliation, and failover machinery may exceed the five-person team's operational capacity even if labeled one logical dependency.
Per-tenant limits alone do not protect aggregate shared capacity from simultaneous compliant bursts; a regional aggregate capacity guard or reserved-headroom mechanism is required.

Adaptive borrowing and redistribution trade false throttling against stale leases, duplicate allocation, oscillation, and partition-time overshoot, and therefore require simulation and a correctness protocol.

The aggregate observation of 4× bursts for under 20 seconds supports investigating burst allowance but does not justify one universal bucket size without tenant-level, regional, concurrency, and endpoint-cost data.
Claims of bounded global quotas remain unproven until retries, failover, stale messages, lease expiry, clock skew, and allocator recovery are handled with explicit invariants and fencing.
A regional limiter is itself a request-path dependency; availability requires an independently resilient topology and explicit degraded behavior for regional store failure.

The comparison against a globally centralized limiter was underspecified. A concrete globally managed design with regional replicas, leased quotas, or degraded local modes must be compared rather than categorically dismissed.
Emergency or degraded-mode ceilings cannot be selected responsibly without quantified capacity headroom and false-throttling tolerances.
Unweighted request-count buckets may not protect shared capacity when endpoint costs differ materially; weighted costs or additional resource guards may be necessary.
The report does not distinguish contractual quota enforcement, tenant fairness, abuse control, and aggregate overload protection, which may require separate hierarchical controls and invariants.
The original 0.95 confidence was too high before trace simulation, failure injection, capacity measurement, benchmarking, and operational assessment.
rejected_criticisms: The criticism that these omissions invalidate the option-level recommendation entirely is not supported by the visible evidence. Among the three stated options, regional bounded quotas remain the best provisional fit for avoiding 180 ms request-path coordination, surviving cross-region partitions, limiting tenant consumption, and accommodating short bursts.

The suggestion that a regional limiter necessarily reproduces the prior regional dependency outage is too strong. It creates that risk, but the outcome depends on deployment topology, reuse of existing infrastructure, replication, and degraded-mode behavior.

The claim that request-count buckets are necessarily unsuitable is not established. Endpoint-cost analysis is missing; weighted charging may be required, but ordinary request tokens could still be adequate if costs correlate sufficiently.
artifact.updated_recommendation: Provisionally select regional token buckets with bounded global quota leases and tenant-specific local burst allowances, but do not approve production implementation until the design defines and validates a numerical global quota invariant, fenced and idempotent lease transfers, atomic regional consumption, failure and recovery semantics, an aggregate regional capacity guard, weighted request costs where needed, and a deployment model that fits the one-stateful-dependency budget. Compare this concrete design quantitatively against a globally managed regional-replica alternative and a simpler regional policy using trace simulation, an 11-minute partition scenario, failure injection, and load benchmarks.
reasons: The supplied evidence disfavors synchronous cross-region enforcement because cross-region control-plane latency is 180 ms p99.

The observed 11-minute regional dependency outage favors local enforcement that can continue without cross-region connectivity, provided the regional limiter itself has suitable availability and degraded modes.
Per-instance uncoordinated buckets provide no stated mechanism for maintaining a tenant-wide bound across instances and autoscaling.
Regional quotas are the most plausible of the three options, but the visible artifacts do not prove their safety, false-throttling rate, or operational fit.

The top 2 percent of tenants generating 61 percent of peak volume strengthens the need for tenant isolation and hot-key testing, while also making correlated-burst and aggregate-capacity controls important.
The criticism changes confidence and implementation gates, not the provisional choice among the three options.

artifact.decision: Provisionally select regional token buckets with bounded global quota leases and local burst allowances, subject to architecture and validation gates before production approval.
artifact.action: Develop and compare a concrete option-3 design using endpoint-weighted per-tenant regional buckets, regional aggregate capacity guards, fenced and idempotent quota leases, atomic consumption, and explicit degraded modes. Approve production only after trace simulation, failure injection, load testing, overshoot analysis for an 11-minute partition, and confirmation that the deployment fits the one-new-stateful-dependency budget.
reasons: Option 3 best fits the stated constraints at the option level: enforcement can remain local during cross-region partitions, avoids a 180 ms p99 cross-region admission path, and can impose tenant-wide bounds that uncoordinated per-instance buckets cannot reliably provide.
Regionally replicated entitlement data supports local quota inputs without adding a synchronous global lookup.
Frequent short bursts justify investigating local burst capacity, but the evidence does not justify a universal 4× allowance or any specific bucket size.
The proposed architecture is not yet production-ready because boundedness, aggregate capacity protection, failure behavior, and operational feasibility remain unproven.
A synchronous centralized limiter is poorly aligned with latency and partition requirements, while independent per-instance buckets lack a defensible global quota invariant.
The strongest criticisms lower confidence and impose implementation gates but do not make either competing option better supported by the visible evidence.
evidence: Problem e3 states that cross-region control-plane round trips have 180 ms p99 latency, favoring request-path-local enforcement.

Problem e4 records an 11-minute regional dependency outage while application instances remained healthy, demonstrating the importance of an independently available limiter path and explicit degraded behavior.
Problem e5 permits at most one new stateful dependency, making operational validation a binding acceptance gate.
Problem e6 states that entitlement data is already replicated regionally and can provide quota inputs without a new global lookup.
Problem e1 states that the top 2% of tenants generate 61% of peak-hour request volume, supporting strong tenant isolation, hot-key testing, and aggregate capacity protection.
Problem e2 states that bursts frequently reach 4× a tenant's five-minute average for less than 20 seconds, supporting investigation of burst absorption but not a universal parameter.
Both reviews independently identify the same material gaps: no numerical quota invariant, no lease/fencing protocol, no aggregate guard, no failure matrix, and no proof of operational fit.
Both rebuttals appropriately retain option 3 only as a provisional choice and reduce confidence to 0.72.
rejected_alternatives: Reject a single synchronous globally centralized limiter as the default because cross-region request-path coordination conflicts with the observed 180 ms p99 latency and the requirement that a regional partition not stop all requests. A concretely replicated global design with local leases remains worth comparison because it may converge with option 3.

Reject uncoordinated per-instance in-memory buckets because their aggregate allowance varies with instance count, autoscaling, restarts, and regional distribution, so they cannot establish a stable tenant-wide bound without additional coordination.

Reject immediate unconditional adoption of option 3 because the visible artifacts do not prove quota boundedness, shared-capacity safety, limiter availability, or compliance with the operational budget.
Reject a universal 4×-for-20-seconds burst policy because only an aggregate observation is supplied; tenant-level distributions, endpoint costs, concurrency, correlation, and headroom are absent.
Reject unrestricted partition-time fail-open behavior because it would undermine tenant isolation and shared-capacity protection.
minority: A concrete globally managed limiter using regional replicas, leased allocations, or local degraded modes may be operationally simpler or equivalent to option 3; the broad option label is underspecified.
A simpler static regional policy may outperform adaptive borrowing if tenant traffic is stable and region-affine.
If quotas are strict contractual, billing, security, or abuse ceilings with zero permissible overshoot, partition-tolerant leased quotas with emergency allowances may be unacceptable.
If endpoint request counts correlate poorly with resource use, weighted tokens alone may be insufficient and direct downstream resource guards may be required.
unresolved: Whether quotas are hard contractual ceilings or soft capacity-management controls.
Acceptable false-throttle rate, global overshoot, admission latency, availability, and protected-capacity headroom.
Tenant-by-region traffic behavior during normal routing changes, retries, evacuation, and correlated bursts.
The numerical invariant covering steady allocations, burst credits, stale leases, transfers, and emergency exposure.
Store topology, atomic consumption, allocator ownership, lease lifecycle, fencing, clock assumptions, recovery, and reconciliation.
Limiter behavior during store timeout, regional store loss, control-plane partition, stale entitlements, and state loss.
Whether the full regional data plane and global control plane count as one supportable stateful dependency.

reasons: Option 3 best fits the stated constraints at the option level: request admission can remain regional during cross-region partitions, avoids a 180 ms p99 cross-region critical path, and can impose tenant-wide bounds that uncoordinated per-instance buckets cannot.
The existing regional entitlement replicas make regional enforcement practical without adding synchronous global entitlement lookups.
Frequent short bursts justify investigating local burst capacity to reduce costly false throttling, but the evidence does not establish a universal bucket size.

The proposal is not yet a production-ready architecture. Its global boundedness, shared-capacity protection, regional failure behavior, and fit within the one-stateful-dependency budget remain unproven.

The rebuttals appropriately retain the provisional option choice while lowering confidence and adding implementation gates; this is better supported than either unconditional adoption or rejecting option 3 solely because details are missing.
evidence: Problem e3 states that cross-region control-plane round trips have 180 ms p99 latency, disfavoring synchronous cross-region admission.
Problem e4 records an 11-minute regional dependency outage while application instances remained healthy, supporting locally autonomous admission with an explicit limiter-failure mode.
Problem e5 limits the team to at most one new stateful dependency, making operational topology a mandatory acceptance gate.
Problem e6 states that entitlement data is already replicated regionally, removing the need for a new synchronous global quota-input lookup.
Problem e1 states that 2% of tenants produce 61% of peak request volume, supporting strong tenant isolation and hot-tenant testing.
Problem e2 states that bursts frequently reach 4× a tenant's five-minute average for less than 20 seconds, supporting investigation of tenant-specific local burst allowances.

Both reviews independently identify the same material gaps: no numerical quota invariant, no proven lease/fencing protocol, no aggregate capacity guard, no failure matrix, and no demonstrated operational fit.
Both rebuttals accept those gaps and reduce confidence to 0.72 while preserving option 3 as the leading conditional choice.
